{{italic title}}
'''''From Zero to Infinity: What Makes Numbers Interesting''''' is a book in [[popular mathematics]] and [[number theory]] by [[Constance Reid]]. It was originally published in 1955 by the Thomas Y. Crowell Company.{{r|gibb}} The fourth edition was published in 1992 by the [[Mathematical Association of America]] in their MAA Spectrum series.{{r|leamy|mor-mor|singmaster}} [[A K Peters]] published a fifth "Fiftieth anniversary edition" in 2006.{{r|belle|godshall|hoagland|lozano-robledo|papp|siegel}}

==Background==
Reid was not herself a professional mathematician, but came from a mathematical family that included her sister [[Julia Robinson]] and brother-in-law [[Raphael M. Robinson]].{{r|reid-obit}} She had worked as a schoolteacher, but by the time of the publication of ''From Zero to Infinity'' she was a "housewife and free-lance writer".{{r|gibb}} She became known for her many books about mathematics and mathematicians, aimed at a popular audience, of which this was the first.{{r|reid-obit}}

Reid's interest in number theory was sparked by her sister's use of computers to discover [[Mersenne prime]]s. She published an article on a closely related topic, [[perfect number]]s, in ''[[Scientific American]]'' in 1953, and wrote this book soon afterward.{{r|singmaster}} Her intended title was ''What Makes Numbers Interesting''; the title ''From Zero to Infinity'' was a change made by the publisher.{{r|lozano-robledo}}

==Topics==
The twelve chapters of ''From Zero to Infinity'' are numbered by the ten decimal digits, <math>e</math> ([[e (mathematical constant)|Euler's number]], approximately 2.71828), and <math>\aleph_0</math>, the [[Aleph number|smallest infinite cardinal number]]. Each chapter's topic is in some way related to its chapter number, with a generally increasing level of sophistication as the book progresses:{{r|singmaster|belle|siegel}}
*Chapter 0 discusses the history of number systems, the development of [[positional notation]] and its need for a placeholder symbol for zero, and the much later understanding of zero as being a number itself. It discusses the special properties held by zero among all other numbers, and the concept of [[indeterminate form]]s arising from [[division by zero]].{{r|singmaster|belle|siegel}}
*Chapter 1 concerns the use of numbers to count things, arithmetic, and the concepts of [[prime number]]s and [[integer factorization]].{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*The topics of Chapter 2 include [[binary representation]], its ancient use in [[peasant multiplication]] and in modern computer arithmetic, and its formalization as a number system by [[Gottfried Leibniz]]. More generally, it discusses the idea of number systems with different bases, and specific bases including [[hexadecimal]].{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*Chapter 3 returns to prime numbers, including the [[sieve of Eratosthenes]] for generating them as well as more modern [[primality test]]s.{{r|singmaster}}
*Chapter 4 concerns [[square number]]s, the observation by [[Galileo]] that squares are [[equinumerous]] with the counting numbers, the [[Pythagorean theorem]], [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], and [[Diophantine equation]]s more generally.{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*Chapter 5 discusses [[figurate number]]s, [[integer partition]]s, and the [[generating function]]s and [[pentagonal number theorem]] that connect these two concepts.{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*In chapter 6, Reid brings in the material from her earlier article on [[perfect number]]s (of which 6 is the smallest nontrivial example), their connection to [[Mersenne prime]]s, the search for [[Largest known prime number|large prime numbers]], and Reid's relatives' discovery of new Mersenne primes.{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*Mersenne primes are the primes one unit less than a [[power of two]]. Chapter 7 instead concerns the primes that are one more than a power of two, the [[Fermat prime]]s, and their close connection to [[constructible polygon]]s. The [[heptagon]], with seven sides, is the smallest polygon that is not constructible, because it is not a product of Fermat primes.{{r|singmaster}}
*Chapter 8 concerns the [[Cube (algebra)|cubes]] and [[Waring's problem]] on representing integers as sums of cubes or other powers.{{r|singmaster|belle}}
*The topic of Chapter 9 is [[modular arithmetic]], [[divisibility]], and their connections to positional notation, including the use of [[casting out nines]] to determine divisibility by nine.{{r|singmaster|belle|siegel}}
*In Chapter <math>e</math>, ''From Zero to Infinity'' shifts from the integers to [[irrational number]]s, [[complex number]]s, [[logarithm]]s, and [[Euler's formula]] <math>e^{i\pi}=1</math>. It connects these topics back to the integers through the theory of [[continued fraction]]s and the [[prime number theorem]].{{r|singmaster}}
*The final chapter, Chapter <math>\aleph_0</math>, provides a basic introduction to [[Aleph number]]s and the theory of infinite sets, including [[Cantor's diagonal argument]] for the existence of uncountable infinite sets.{{r|singmaster|belle}}

The first edition included only chapters 0 through 9.{{r|gibb}} The chapter on infinite sets was added in the second edition, replacing a section on the [[interesting number paradox]].{{r|hamilton}} Later editions of the book were "thoroughly updated" by Reid;{{r|singmaster}} in particular, the fifth edition includes updates on the search for [[Mersenne prime]]s and the proof of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], and restores an index that had been dropped from earlier editions.{{r|papp}}

==Audience and reception==
''From Zero to Infinity'' has been written to be accessible both to students and non-mathematical adults,{{r|singmaster}} requiring only high-school level mathematics as background.{{r|hoagland}} Short sets of "quiz questions" at the end chapter could be helpful in sparking classroom discussions, making this useful as supplementary material for secondary-school mathematics courses.{{r|godshall|siegel}}

In reviewing the fourth edition, mathematician [[David Singmaster]] describes it as "one of the classic works of mathematical popularisation since its initial appearance", and "a delightful introduction to what mathematics is about".{{r|singmaster}} Reviewer Lynn Godshall calls it "a highly-readable history of numbers", "easily understood by both educators and their students alike".{{r|godshall}} Murray Siegel describes it as a must have for "the library of every mathematics teacher, and university faculty who prepare students to teach mathematics".{{r|siegel}}

Singmaster complains only about two pieces of mathematics in the book: the assertion in chapter 4 that the Egyptians were familiar with the 3-4-5 right triangle (still the subject of considerable scholarly debate) and the omission from chapter 7 of any discussion of why classifying [[constructible polygon]]s can be reduced to the case of prime numbers of sides.{{r|singmaster}} Siegel points out another small error, on algebraic factorization, but suggests that finding it could make another useful exercise for students.{{r|siegel}}
